sections.body:
A **digital nomad** is someone who works for money that does not depend on being in a particular country, and who uses that freedom to live in more than one place over a year. The definition has two halves and both matter. The first half is about the work: your income comes from a client, a platform or a salary that follows you across borders. The second half is about the movement: you actually change country, often every few months, and you build your life around that rather than around one place.

What separates a digital nomad from other people who work while travelling is duration and repeatability. A tourist who answers emails from a hotel for two weeks is on holiday. A person who stays three months in Lisbon, then three in Chiang Mai, then three in Mexico City, with a calendar that repeats, is a digital nomad. The pattern is the thing.

It is worth being precise about who is not one. An **expat** is someone who relocates for a fixed period and then settles in one country, usually with a local work permit. A **remote worker** may live in one place for years and simply work from home. A **travelling professional** moves because of a company rotation or a project. A **digital nomad** moves on their own schedule, keeps the income portable, and usually holds a visa that explicitly allows remote work.

The scale is now large enough that this is not a subculture of a few hundred people. Portugal, Spain, Estonia, Japan, Thailand, Mexico, Croatia and dozens of other countries run **nomad visa** schemes specifically for this group, and the number of countries offering one keeps growing. The result is a new social class with its own economy: short-term apartments, coworking spaces, community meetups, and a set of shared unwritten rules about how to behave in a country you are only passing through.

Read the rest of this article as the practical side of that new class: what makes it work, what the law requires, and what goes wrong for people who do not check.
examples: I work for clients in three countries, so I move when the work allows it.
This is a nomad visa, so I can stay here for a year and work remotely.
sections.heading: What a digital nomad actually is

sections.body:
Location-independent work rests on four conditions. When one of them fails, the whole arrangement fails with it.

The first is **portable income**. Your money must arrive somewhere that does not depend on your address, and it must survive a currency change. A salary paid into one local bank account is not portable, because it stops when you leave. Payment platforms, foreign currency accounts and international transfer services solve this. The second is **connectivity**. A sold-out café or a mobile hotspot with a daily data cap is not a working environment. Nomads plan around upload speed and whether calls are stable, because a video meeting that freezes is a professional problem, not a small one.

The third is **legal permission**. Almost every country distinguishes between working for a local employer, which needs a work permit, and working for a foreign employer or client from abroad, which many countries still restrict. This is the single biggest legal difference between a nomad and an ordinary remote worker. Some countries have no clear rule at all, which means the risk is yours. The fourth is **a workable daily life**: somewhere to sit, a bed, and enough stability to sleep.

Notice that the fourth condition is the one people underestimate. The infrastructure of a city matters more than its photographs. A cheap city with no workspaces, no cafés that allow laptops and no reliable power is more expensive in practice than a slightly dearer one with a good coworking space and a monthly rate.

The practical consequence is that the four conditions are checked in order. Money first, then the law, then the connection, then the city. People usually do it the other way round, fall in love with a place on a photograph, and then discover the visa does not exist.
examples: My income has to reach an account that works in every country I visit.
Check the visa rule before you look at apartments, not after.
sections.heading: The four things that make it possible

sections.body:
This is the part that turns an exciting plan into a legal problem. Two separate systems apply, and confusing them is how people end up in trouble.

The **visa** question is: may a person on this status work at all, and for whom? Nomad visas usually require proof of remote income above a threshold, health insurance, a clean criminal record, and sometimes evidence of income for the whole stay. Tourist visas almost always forbid working, and a short course of online freelancing counted as work is a real rule, not a technicality.

The **tax** question is separate and more dangerous: where are you tax resident? Tax residence usually depends on where you spend most of your time, where your family is, where your home is, and where your centre of interests is. Stay in a country more than 183 days and many countries will treat you as tax resident there, whether or not you have a visa. Some countries also tax foreign income earned while you are there.

You also have to watch the rules of the country you are leaving. A few countries tax citizens on worldwide income regardless of where they live, and several charge an exit fee when you leave permanently.

Three practical habits prevent nearly all of this. First, keep a **travel log**: every day you are in a country, with the entry and exit dates. Second, talk to a qualified accountant or a tax adviser in the country whose rules are about to affect you, and pay for the hour rather than guessing. Third, keep evidence of your income and of where it was earned.

None of this makes the lifestyle impossible. It makes it a little less spontaneous, which is the actual price of working abroad.
examples: I stayed 190 days last year, so I need to check the tax position there.
Does this visa let me work for a client who is not registered in this country?
sections.heading: The visa and tax questions you must answer first

sections.body:
These terms come up in visa applications, lease agreements and community boards, and each one has a precise job.

A **nomad visa** is a residence permit issued to people who work remotely for foreign employers or clients. A **digital nomad** is the person holding it, though the word is also used loosely for anyone who works while travelling. **Tax residency** is the status that decides which country has a claim on your income. A **statutory residency** or **183-day rule** is a common threshold used in many tax treaties to start counting days in a country.

Earned income means money from work you do. **Passive income** means money from assets such as a rented flat or a portfolio. Some nomad visas accept passive income and some do not, so the distinction decides whether you qualify.

A **co-working space** is a paid desk-and-workspace arrangement, usually by the day or the month. **Coliving** is a building where people rent a room and share a kitchen and common areas, and it is the most common way nomads find a social life. **Slow travel** is the practice of staying in one place for weeks or months instead of moving every few days. A **digital nomad community** is the local network of people in the same position, found through meetups, coworking spaces and online groups.

Offsiting is the opposite of working from home: you take your job to a shared space other than your own flat. **Burnout** is the exhaustion that comes from working with no separation between work and life. **Nomad tax trap** is the informal name for the mistake of treating every country as a tax-free zone.
examples: The nomad visa accepts passive income as well as earned income.
Check the tax residency rules before you stay past 90 days.
sections.heading: The words of the nomad economy

terms.example: As a digital nomad, I move when the client contract ends.
terms.gloss: Someone who earns income that does not depend on one country and who lives in several places over a year.

terms.example: The nomad visa requires proof of income above a monthly threshold.
terms.gloss: A residence permit for people who work remotely for foreign employers or clients without a local work permit.

terms.example: Tax residency is the part nobody checks before they book the flight.
terms.gloss: The status that decides which country has a claim to tax your income, usually based on where you spend most of your time.

terms.example: I took a room in a coliving for a month and made friends in a week.
terms.gloss: A building where residents rent a room and share a kitchen and common areas, and where nomads often find a community.

terms.example: A co-working space costs less than the coffee I would buy sitting in a café all day.
terms.gloss: A paid workspace where people work in the same room, usually by the day or the month, with a desk and reliable internet.

terms.example: Slow travel costs less and lets you actually know the place.
terms.gloss: Staying in one place for weeks or months instead of moving on every few days, which is what makes long-term work possible.

terms.example: My company gave me an offsiting budget of two hundred dollars a month.
terms.gloss: Working from a shared space other than your own home, which many employers offer or pay for.

sections.body:
The comparison always comes down to the same five things, in this order.

Cost of living is the first, and it is not the monthly rent. Add the deposit, the monthly utility bill, the local transport pass, one week of groceries, a coworking desk, two flights home, and the cost of a single coffee per working day. Many cities that look cheap become expensive once you add flights and the fact that you cannot cook at home.

Time zone is second and it is a professional question, not a lifestyle one. If your colleagues are in one time zone, an eight-hour difference means your working day overlaps by one hour or not at all. Six hours or more usually means you either work a split day or you negotiate a rotation with your team. People often survive an ugly schedule for a month and then quit.

Connectivity is third. Check the actual upload speed on a normal working day, not the headline number. Ask a local whether the connection is stable at 09:00 and 17:00, and whether power cuts happen. Then check whether calls work well from the place you are considering to rent. A video call every morning is a hard requirement in most remote jobs.

Community is fourth. A city with a large established nomad community gives you friends, a doctor who knows your history, a group of people to eat with on a Tuesday, and advice about which neighbourhoods are safe. This is worth more than a better apartment.

Everyday life is fifth: the weather you will live in for three months, the food you can actually eat, how safe the street is at night, and whether the pace suits you. You cannot work well in a place that makes you miserable, however cheap it is.
examples: Eight hours of time difference is a lot, so I need to talk to my team about the hours.
I checked the upload speed during the evening, not at lunchtime.
sections.heading: Choosing a city: five things that decide it

sections.body:
A month somewhere is a good length: long enough to work properly, short enough to be reversible. This is the order that works.

Do the legal and money checks first, because they can end the plan before you spend anything. Then do the housing, because the best rent in a city is in an area you have not visited yet.
examples: I am booking two weeks first, then I will look at monthly rentals on the ground.
Let us agree the overlap hours in writing, so nobody expects a reply at midnight.
sections.heading: How to plan a month in a new city
steps: Check the visa rules for your passport and confirm what work is allowed.
Confirm your tax position and note the day count in every country you visit.
Ask your employer or clients about the hours you are expected to overlap.
Check the upload speed on a normal working day, in the morning and the evening.
Budget the month in full: rent, deposit, utilities, workspace, flights, food.
Book a place for the first two weeks, then look for a monthly rental in person.
Set up the routine, the gym, the doctor and one recurring social habit.
Write down the exit date and what you will do when you leave.

sections.body: Watch for these four. The first is **working on a tourist visa**: in many countries that is illegal, and it can lead to fines, deportation or a future visa refusal. The second is **ignoring the day count**: the 183-day threshold is the rule that catches people who thought each stay was separate. The third is **the deposit trap**: a monthly apartment can require three months of rent plus a month as deposit, and the deposit may not be returnable if you leave early. The fourth is **unlimited data plans and visa-run advice** sold online: some of it is outdated, some of it is illegal, and a border run can still count your days. When a rule matters, read the official government page, not a forum post.
examples: This permit says remote work only, and it says which clients I may serve.
I am keeping a day count, because I do not want to argue with a tax office later.
sections.heading: The traps that cost nomads real money

sections.body:
The job itself is rarely the hard part. The hard part is the shape of the day when your flat, your clients and your social life are in different countries.

The first requirement is a **boundary**. Working from home means work follows you around: the laptop on the kitchen table, the notification during dinner, the reply you send from bed at midnight. Nomads who last a year all build some kind of separation, usually a coworking space for the middle of the day, a fixed stopping time, and a rule about when the work chat is allowed to open.

The second requirement is **a reliable routine**. One of the strongest habits is to keep the same working hours wherever you are, because your body clock and your clients both rely on them. When you fly, keep your laptop on your home time for the first two or three days if you have a meeting the next morning.

The third is **the team side of remote work**. Write things down. Agree on hours in writing. Do not rely on being online, because you will be online in the wrong hours for somebody. Say what you can commit to, then do exactly that: reliability across time zones matters more than hours of presence.

The fourth is **money administration**, which sounds dull and is the thing that ruins months. Set aside the tax money the moment it arrives, keep separate accounts for spending and for the tax fund, and get the paperwork organised as you go. A nomad with no records at tax time is a nomad with a problem.
examples: I work from the co-working space between ten and four, and my phone is off after that.
I agreed the overlap hours in writing, so nobody expects a reply at midnight.
sections.heading: How the working day actually works

sections.body:
The social media version of this life is a balcony, a laptop and a coffee. The real version has two hard parts, and both are normal rather than signs that you chose badly.

The first is **loneliness**. Working alone from a rented flat in a city where you know nobody produces a specific kind of quiet that is hard to talk about, because it happens to people who seem to be doing well. The fix is boring and effective: one recurring thing with the same people. A coworking desk in the same room every day, a running club on Sunday, a language class on Wednesday evening, a weekly dinner with the same four people. One fixed habit beats a new country every month.

The second is the **end of the nomad year**. The dream is to keep going, and many people reach month seven with savings, a good routine and no reason to stop. Then the practical questions arrive: where do you register your company, which country's health insurance covers you, where do you pay tax, where do you keep your belongings, and where are you actually living?

Two ways of handling it. The first is to plan a **base**: one country where you keep a home, a mailbox, a bank account and a tax residence, and from which you travel. The second is to **stop on purpose**: choose a city, take a local lease for a year, and use the nomad years as a series of seasons rather than a permanent state.

Neither is failure. Both are the difference between a lifestyle that lasts ten years and one that lasts ten months.
examples: I keep a flat in my home country as a base and travel out of it.
I booked the same desk in the same co-working space every day, and that is what fixed it.
sections.heading: The part nobody posts about

item.summary: Working from another country is now possible for tens of millions of people, but it is governed by visa rules, tax rules and the cost of daily life. After reading this you can tell a genuine digital nomad from a tourist working online, check what you must do before you move, and pick a city that fits your work and your budget.
item.title: Digital Nomads: Working From Anywhere
